chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Husaynayn, from al-Nadr ibn Shu'ayb, from Abd al-Ghaffar al-Jazzi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

I asked him about a man who died while he had a debt upon him. He said: 'If it was taken from his body [his estate], and paid out without waste, Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, will not hold him accountable, provided He knows from his intention that he intended to pay. Except for one who did not intend to pay from his trust, for he is like the thief. And likewise the zakat, and likewise one who makes it permissible to take away the dowries of the women.'

key_terms.الْأَمَانَةُ: The trust (referring to the debt owed)
key_terms.الْبَدَنُ: The body (referring to the estate/property of the deceased)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a deceased person's unpaid debts and their spiritual accountability?
ai.summary: In this ruling from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) clarifies that unpaid debts are settled from the deceased's estate, absolving them of accountability if they possessed the sincere intention to pay. The hadith further emphasizes the gravity of misappropriating trusts by likening intentional defaulters to thieves, extending this principle to zakat and dowries, which underscores the Shia legal emphasis on the sanctity of financial obligations and the continuity of personal accountability through estate distribution.
